title: Path Params, Query Params, Headers, and Bodies
summary: Read every part of a request, from path and query parameters to headers and JSON bodies, and shape the JSON you send back.
intro: A route gets a request to the right handler. Then the handler has to read it: which room, which filters, which page, who's asking, and what they sent. That information arrives in five places, each with its own rules, and almost everything a client sends arrives as plain text that your code has to turn into real values. Read it carelessly, and you get the classic API bugs: lists that skip items, a body that's silently ignored, an update that wipes a field. This lesson goes through each place in turn, the path, the query string, the headers, and the body, then ends with the other half of the job: the JSON Roombook sends back.

steps.title: Where request data lives
steps.body:
Every piece of information in a request has a place where it belongs, and putting it in the right one isn't just tidiness. Caches, logs, browsers, and proxies all treat each place differently, so the place decides who sees the data, what gets saved, and what can be bookmarked or shared.

```diagram request-data-parts
Each place has one job. Everything but the body arrives as plain text.
```

## Five places, five jobs

- **The path** says which thing: `/v1/rooms/3` is room 3. It's the resource's identity, so it's what gets bookmarked, linked, and cached.
- **The query string**, the part after `?`, holds options for reading: which rooms to include, in what order, which page. `/v1/rooms?building=main-library` is still the list of rooms, seen through a filter.
- **Headers** describe the request itself: what format the body is in, what format the client wants back, who's calling, and conditions like only if it changed.
- **The body** carries the content of a POST, PUT, or PATCH: the booking to make, the fields to change.
- **Cookies** carry the session, recall from the web course: the browser sends them back in a `Cookie` header on every request to the site. The lesson on logins builds Roombook's sessions on them.

One rule follows from this: never put secrets in the URL. Paths and query strings end up in server logs, in browser history, and in the logs of every proxy along the way. Passwords, tokens, and keys go in headers, which those tools don't save by default.

## Where Go puts each one

| Place | In Go | For `/v1/rooms/3?limit=20` |
|---|---|---|
| Path parameters | `r.PathValue(name)` | `r.PathValue("roomID")` is `"3"` |
| Query string | `r.URL.Query()` | `.Get("limit")` is `"20"` |
| Headers | `r.Header.Get(name)` | `r.Header.Get("Accept")` |
| Body | `r.Body` | a stream you decode yourself |
| Cookies | `r.Cookie(name)` | the lesson on logins uses it |

Go parses the path and the query string when you ask, and leaves the body as a stream: data that arrives in chunks, which your code reads, here with `encoding/json`.

## It's all text

Look at the values in that table: `"3"` and `"20"`, in quotes. The path, the query string, and the headers are plain text, every character of them, so Go can only hand you strings. Turning them into numbers, dates, and lists is your job, with packages like `strconv`, and it's where many bugs start: Go won't compare `"20"` with a number, which is a mercy, but `"20" < "3"` is true, since strings compare letter by letter.

The JSON body is the one exception. JSON has its own types, numbers, true and false, null, lists, and objects, so decoding into a struct gives you real values: `{"attendees": 3}` fills an `int` field with 3. Decoding into `any` instead gives Go's default types, and every JSON number becomes a `float64`, even 3. That's one reason Roombook always decodes into structs. JSON has no type for dates, but a `time.Time` field reads a time written as text, like `"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z"`. And the client chose every value, so a field you expect might be missing. The lesson on validation and errors checks every value at the edge, and this lesson shows where each one comes from.

The examples make all of this visible, with a small server that answers with exactly what it received.

examples.title: A server that echoes what it got
examples.prompt: A demo, not part of Roombook: `cmd/echodemo/main.go`, run with `go run ./cmd/echodemo` while Roombook is stopped. It sends back the parts of each POST it receives.
examples.explanation: The handler decodes the body into a map of `any`, so it accepts any JSON object, then answers with a struct written right where it's used, a common Go habit for one-off shapes. It copies in the path parameter, the parsed query string, one header, and the body. `%T` prints the Go type of a value, which shows what decoding into `any` made of the number. `json.NewEncoder(w).Encode` writes JSON straight to the response, with a line break at the end. The next example sends it a request.

examples.title: Sending it every kind of data
examples.prompt: One request with a path parameter, two query parameters, one of them twice, and a JSON body. The quotes around the URL stop the terminal from reading `&` as its own symbol.
examples.explanation: `roomID` is `"3"`, a string, though it looks like a number. In the query, every value is a list of strings, even `date`, which appeared once: `r.URL.Query()` returns a `url.Values`, a map from each name to all its values. `amenity` appeared twice, so its list has both, which the next part relies on. `content-type` was found even though curl sent `Content-Type`, since header names ignore capital letters. In the body, `note` is a real `null`, and `attendees` is 3, but stored as a `float64`.

steps.title: Query parameters: filters, sorting, and pages

examples.title: Filtering by building and amenity
examples.prompt: Rooms in the Main Library that have a whiteboard. The URL is in quotes because of the `&`.
examples.explanation: Hopper is in the Science Library, so the building filter dropped it. Lovelace and Turing both have a whiteboard. They come back sorted by name, the default, so Lovelace is first. Both fit on one page of 20, so `nextCursor` is `null`: there's nothing more to fetch. In Go, the list is a struct with a `NextCursor *string` field, and a `nil` pointer turns into `null`. A client checks that one field to know whether to ask again.

examples.title: Two pages, two rooms at a time
examples.prompt: The first command sorts by capacity with pages of 2. The second sends back the `nextCursor` the first one returned.
examples.explanation: The first page holds the two smallest rooms, Lovelace with 4 and Turing with 6, and a cursor. Decoded, the cursor is `{"after":[6,1]}`: after the room with capacity 6 and id 1, which is Turing. The second page starts right after it, with Hopper, and its `nextCursor` is `null`, since that was the last room. Each answer ends in a line break, from `writeJSON`, so the two print on separate lines.

examples.title: A limit over the maximum
examples.prompt: Ask for 500 rooms in one page.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:54 GMT
Content-Length: 68

{"status":422,"title":"limit must be a whole number from 1 to 100"}
examples.explanation: The request was fine to read, a query string with a number in it, but the number broke Roombook's rule, so the answer is a 422 whose title says what's allowed. Go writes the code's older name, Unprocessable Entity, and the number is what counts. Quietly using 100 instead would have been the other choice, and it hides the client's mistake: they'd think they got everything.

steps.title: Headers: about the request and the answer
steps.body:
Headers are where a request and a response describe themselves: what format they're in, who's asking, and under what conditions. They're easy to overlook, since curl hides them unless you ask, and they're behind some of an API's most useful tricks, like answering a repeated read with no body at all.

## Request headers Roombook reads

| Header | What it says | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `Content-Type` | the format of the body | `application/json` |
| `Accept` | the formats the client can read | `application/json` |
| `Authorization` | the caller's credentials | `Bearer eyJhbGciOi...` |
| `If-None-Match` | send it only if it changed | `"2fd79f95d0da1eef"` |
| `If-Match` | change it only if it hasn't changed | `"3"` |
| `Idempotency-Key` | a retry of an earlier request | `9f1c2e7a-...` |

The lesson on logins reads `Authorization`, the lesson on constraints and transactions uses `If-Match`, and the reliability lesson uses `Idempotency-Key`. In Go, `r.Header.Get("Idempotency-Key")` returns a header's value, or `""` when it's missing.

## Response headers Roombook sends

| Header | What it says |
|---|---|
| `Location` | where the new or moved resource is |
| `Cache-Control` | who may keep a copy of the answer, and for how long |
| `ETag` | a fingerprint of this version of the resource |
| `Retry-After` | how long to wait before trying again, after a 429 or 503 |

`Cache-Control` suits data that rarely changes. Roombook's buildings change about once a year, so the list, in `internal/api/buildings.go`, says any cache may keep it for five minutes:

```go
func listBuildings(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=300")
	writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, buildingList{Items: buildings})
}
```

`public` means any cache along the way may store it, and `max-age=300` means for 300 seconds. Answers that depend on who's asking, like a user's own bookings, must never be `public`, or a shared cache could hand one person's bookings to another. For those, use `private` or `no-store`, which the Redis lesson comes back to.

## Two rules for names

Header names ignore capital letters: `Content-Type`, `content-type`, and `CONTENT-TYPE` are the same header. Go stores them in one **canonical** spelling, with a capital letter at the start of each word, so `Get` and `Set` find a header however you write its name. That's also why Go sends `Etag` where you wrote `ETag`, as the first example shows, which every client accepts. HTTP/2, recall from the web course, even sends every name in lowercase.

A header you invent needs no `X-` at the start. That prefix was once the custom for headers outside the standards, but headers that started as `X-` and later became standard had to keep the awkward name forever, so the custom was dropped in 2012. That's why it's `Idempotency-Key`, not `X-Idempotency-Key`. You'll still meet old ones like `X-Request-Id`, which the middleware lesson uses because everyone already does.

## ETag and 304: nothing new to send

An **ETag** is a fingerprint of the body. A client that saved the room, and its ETag, can later ask for it again with `If-None-Match` and the fingerprint. If the room is unchanged, the server answers **304 Not Modified** with no body: your copy is still good. If it changed, the client gets a normal 200 with the new room and a new ETag. That saves the bandwidth of the body, which matters on a phone, and browsers do it on their own for anything they've cached.

Go adds no ETags by itself, so `GET /v1/rooms/{roomID}` uses a helper in `json.go`:

```go
func writeJSONWithETag(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, v any) {
	body, err := json.Marshal(v)
	if err != nil {
		http.Error(w, "internal server error", http.StatusInternalServerError)
		return
	}
	sum := sha256.Sum256(body)
	etag := `"` + hex.EncodeToString(sum[:8]) + `"`
	w.Header().Set("ETag", etag)
	if r.Header.Get("If-None-Match") == etag {
		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNotModified)
		return
	}
	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
	w.Write(append(body, '\n'))
}
```

`sha256.Sum256` makes a **hash**, a short value computed from the bytes that changes completely if any byte changes. The first 8 of its 32 bytes, written in hexadecimal and wrapped in quotes, are plenty for a fingerprint. Because it covers the exact bytes, it's a **strong** ETag. One marked `W/`, a **weak** ETag, promises only the same meaning. A real client may send several ETags in one `If-None-Match`, or `*`, and a complete helper checks for those too. The helper never calls `WriteHeader` for a 200, since writing a body without it sends 200 by itself.

It doesn't save the server's work, since it built the whole answer to fingerprint it. The lesson on constraints and transactions gives each room a version number, which makes an ETag Roombook can check without building the body, and lets `If-Match` stop two people's edits from overwriting each other.

examples.title: Asking again with If-None-Match
examples.prompt: The first command reads room 1 and shows its ETag. The second sends that ETag back.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Etag: "2fd79f95d0da1eef"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:54 GMT
Content-Length: 100

{"id":1,"name":"Turing","building":"main-library","capacity":6,"amenities":["whiteboard","screen"]}
HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
Etag: "2fd79f95d0da1eef"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:54 GMT
examples.explanation: The first answer is a full 200 with the room, 100 bytes, and its ETag, sent as `Etag` because of Go's canonical spelling. The second is a 304 with the same ETag and no body, since the room hadn't changed. The quotes are part of the ETag, which is why the header in the command has double quotes inside single ones. Change the room with a PATCH, and the same second command gets a 200 again, with the new room and a new fingerprint.

examples.title: The buildings list, with Cache-Control
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:54 GMT
Content-Length: 276

{"items":[{"id":1,"slug":"main-library","name":"Main Library","timezone":"America/New_York","opensAt":"08:00","closesAt":"22:00"},{"id":2,"slug":"science-library","name":"Science Library","timezone":"America/New_York","opensAt":"09:00","closesAt":"18:00"}],"nextCursor":null}
examples.explanation: `Cache-Control` is there, as the handler set it before `writeJSON`. A browser that calls this from a web page keeps the answer for five minutes, and repeats within that time never reach Roombook at all. Each building has its slug, the name the rooms filter uses, and its opening hours, written as local times in the building's time zone, `America/New_York`, which later lessons need to check that a booking falls inside them.

steps.title: The request body

examples.title: A form post instead of JSON
examples.prompt: `-d` on its own sends the body as form data, the way an HTML form would.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 415 Unsupported Media Type
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:54 GMT
Content-Length: 43

{"status":415,"title":"Body must be JSON"}
examples.explanation: curl sent `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `decodeJSON` saw a type that isn't JSON, and the room was never created. The 415 and its title tell the client's developer exactly what to fix: send JSON. The body wasn't even read, since checking a header costs nothing and reading a body can cost a lot.

examples.title: Too big, broken, and too much
examples.prompt: `big.json` is a 200 KB booking with a very long note, saved in the folder you run curl from. The second body is JSON cut off halfway, and the third is two JSON values. `-w '%{http_code}\n'` prints only the status code.
examples.explanation: The `@` in `--json @big.json` tells curl to send the file's contents. Reading stopped at 100 KB, and the answer was 413, titled `Body must be 100 KB or less`, with no booking made. The cut-off body got a 400, since it couldn't be parsed at all, and so did the one with a second value after the first. That's the 400 and 422 split from the routes lesson: 400 when the request can't be read, 422 when it can, and a value breaks a rule.

examples.title: Keeping a note, then clearing it
examples.prompt: Booking 1002 has the note Chemistry revision. The first patch leaves the note out, and the second sets it to null.
examples.code:
curl -X PATCH --json '{"attendees": 4}' http://localhost:8080/v1/bookings/1002
curl -X PATCH --json '{"note": null}' http://localhost:8080/v1/bookings/1002
examples.explanation: After the first patch, `attendees` is 4 and the note is untouched, since `Note.Set` stayed false. After the second, the note is `null`, since the field was there with `null` as its value, so `Set` was true and `Value` was `nil`. `version` went up with each change, as the store's `Update` does every time. Booking 1002 comes from the next part's first example, so create it first if your server restarted.

steps.title: Responses and the handler's job
steps.body:
A handler's last step, the response, is the contract clients code against. Every field name, every time format, and every null is something a web app or a phone app will depend on, and changing it later breaks them. So Roombook decides these once, and every handler follows the same rules.

## Parse, check, act, respond

Every handler does the same four things, in this order:

1. **Parse**: turn the request's text into values, like an id from the path or a `RoomQuery` from the query string.
2. **Check**: refuse what's wrong, with the right code, before changing anything. Is the id valid, is the room there, are the values allowed.
3. **Act**: do the work, usually through the store.
4. **Respond**: turn the result into JSON, with the right status and headers.

Keeping that order means a request that fails a check never changes anything, so an error never leaves half a booking behind. The lesson on validation and errors moves the parse and check steps into validation, and the lesson on services and repositories moves the act step into a service, but the order stays.

## Roombook's JSON rules

- **Field names are camelCase**, like `startsAt` and `roomId`, the style of most JSON APIs. Go's field names are capitalized, `StartsAt`, so every field gets a JSON tag with the name the contract uses.
- **Times are strings in RFC 3339 format, in UTC, to the second**, like `"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z"`. RFC 3339 is the standard way to write a date and time, and the `Z` at the end means UTC, the time zone with no offset. One zone for every time means a client never has to guess.
- **Ids are whole numbers**, like `1002`, held in Go as `int64`.
- **Every field is always there.** A note that's empty is `"note": null`, never a missing field. A client can rely on the shape without checking first whether a field exists.
- **Lists are objects**: `{"items": [...], "nextCursor": ...}`, even when there's only one page.

The last two rules mean Roombook's views use no `omitempty`, the tag option that leaves a field out when it's empty. `omitempty` can't even tell when a `time.Time` is unset, since a struct is never empty to it, and Go 1.24 added `omitzero` for that case, which leaves out a field holding its zero value. They're useful for other JSON, and wrong for a contract that promises every field.

## Never send what you store

From this lesson on, `domain.Booking` is the booking as Roombook stores it, with no JSON tags at all, and with fields that aren't part of the contract, like `CancelledAt`, the moment a booking was cancelled, which Roombook keeps for its own records. So no handler sends a stored booking as it is. Each one passes through a **view**, a struct that's exactly the JSON the contract promises, built by a function, in `internal/api/bookings.go`:

```go
func toBookingResponse(b domain.Booking) bookingResponse {
	return bookingResponse{
		ID:        b.ID,
		RoomID:    b.RoomID,
		UserID:    b.UserID,
		StartsAt:  b.StartsAt.UTC().Truncate(time.Second),
		EndsAt:    b.EndsAt.UTC().Truncate(time.Second),
		Attendees: b.Attendees,
		Note:      b.Note,
		Status:    string(b.Status),
		Version:   b.Version,
		CreatedAt: b.CreatedAt.UTC().Truncate(time.Second),
	}
}
```

`bookingResponse` has the JSON tags: `json:"startsAt"`, and so on. Every handler that answers with a booking calls it: `writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, toBookingResponse(b))`. Since it lists each field by name, `CancelledAt` stays inside, and a new field added to storage later, like a user's password hash in the lesson on logins, can never leak into a response by accident. It's also where the time rules live, in one place. A `time.Time` keeps the offset it was parsed with, and would write `+02:00` back out, so `UTC()` converts it, and `Truncate(time.Second)` drops any fraction of a second. Go writes a fraction only when there is one, so whole seconds come out exactly as the contract wants. And the view lets storage change without changing the API, which is what the PostgreSQL lesson will need when the records come from a database.

## Accept and 406

A client says which formats it can read in the `Accept` header. Roombook only speaks JSON, so a client that accepts only, say, `text/csv` can't be served, and the honest answer is **406 Not Acceptable**. Most clients send `Accept: application/json` or `*/*`, which means anything, so Roombook can leave this check out until it ever offers a second format.

Some chores belong to every request, like an id and a log line, and the next lesson, on middleware, does them once for all of them.

examples.title: A booking made in another time zone
examples.prompt: A student's phone set to UTC+2 sends local times, written with a `+02:00` offset.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /v1/bookings/1002
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:54 GMT
Content-Length: 210

{"id":1002,"roomId":2,"userId":1,"startsAt":"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z","endsAt":"2026-10-05T15:00:00Z","attendees":2,"note":"Chemistry revision","status":"confirmed","version":1,"createdAt":"2026-10-01T09:00:00Z"}
examples.explanation: Decoding read each time into a `time.Time`, which understands the offset, and the view wrote it back in UTC: 16:00 at UTC+2 is 14:00 UTC. The client sent one format, and every client reads the same format back. The handler also stores the times as UTC, with `in.StartsAt.UTC()`, so the stored booking and its view agree. `createdAt` is Roombook's story clock, 1 October 2026 at 9:00 UTC, which stands in for the real time until the testing lesson shows how to control time in code.

examples.title: Reading a booking through its view
examples.prompt: The seeded booking, Ada's study group in Turing.
examples.explanation: Every field the contract promises is there, in the order the view struct lists them, in camelCase, with every time in UTC. Monday 5 October from 14:00 to 15:30 UTC is a 90-minute booking, on the 30-minute boundaries Roombook's rules require. The same view serves the GET, the POST, the PATCH, and the cancel action, so all four answers have the same shape, and a client needs only one type for a booking.

recap:
- The path names the thing, the query string holds options, headers describe the request, the body carries content, and cookies carry the session.
- Path, query, and headers arrive as text, so turn them into real values with strconv, and never put secrets in a URL.
- r.URL.Query() gives each name a slice of values, so repeated names like amenity arrive together.
- Give list parameters defaults and bounds, sort from an allowlist, and page with an opaque cursor, not an offset.
- Header names ignore case, new ones need no X- prefix, and an ETag with If-None-Match gives a 304 with no body.
- decodeJSON accepts only JSON, with 415 for other types, 413 past 100 KB, and 400 for broken JSON or data after it.
- A generic Optional type with a Set flag tells a missing field from a null one, so a PATCH can clear a value.
- Send camelCase JSON with UTC times to the second and every field present, built by a view, never the stored record.
